stances.claim: Imelda was acquitted not because she was innocent but because the prosecution committed critical evidentiary failures: testimonies constituted hearsay since witnesses had no personal knowledge of Swiss document contents and could not authenticate Swiss officials' signatures.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidentiary-failure explanation distinguishing factual guilt from legal proof

stances.claim: The 'existence-but-not-truth' stipulation was worthless -- 'like agreeing to the existence of a witness but not to the truth of his/her testimony' -- guaranteeing the documents could not serve as substantive evidence.

The solution was obvious and accessible: take depositions of Swiss officials who issued or certified the documents -- since both Del Rosario and Chavez regularly traveled to Switzerland -- making the failure inexcusable.

Justice Leonen's conclusion that the prosecution 'could have done better. Sadly, it failed' frames the acquittal as an institutional indictment of prosecution quality, not a vindication of Marcos wrongdoing.

notable_anecdotes: The opening media-question cascade -- 'Did she not brag to media that they own everything in the Philippines? Who bungled her case?' -- framing public indignation before providing the legally grounded answer.
The 14 intransferable hearing dates in January-February 2007 individually listed -- and Chavez absent for nearly all -- physicalizing prosecutorial neglect through calendar specificity.

Prosecutor Yarte being at a prosecutors' convention in Boracay on the exact day Chavez attended (April 11) and needed to identify vital documents -- the single most absurd prosecutorial coordination failure in the entire chronology.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers friends' indignant questions about why Imelda Marcos was acquitted in the Swiss-funds case upheld by the Supreme Court in Chavez v. Marcos (June 27, 2018, J. Leonen). After the 1986 EDSA revolution, Swiss magistrate Cosenday froze Marcos Swiss accounts and the Swiss Federal SC gave the PH government one year to file cases. SolGen Chavez filed criminal cases in the RTC for violation of the foreign currency account ban, presenting PCGG Commissioner Del Rosario and Chavez himself as witnesses on Swiss bank papers. Chavez missed nearly all of 14 intransferable hearing dates; on April 11 he attended but could not identify vital documents because prosecutor Yarte was at a Boracay convention; a PCGG lawyer then appeared with a DOJ letter causing contentious authority disputes. Imelda's lawyer Sison stipulated on the 'existence' but not the 'truth' of the documents -- what CJ calls a 'worthless' concession 'like agreeing to the existence of a witness but not to the truth of his/her testimony.' Judge Pampilo acquitted Imelda on March 10, 2008: testimonies were hearsay since witnesses could not authenticate Swiss officials' signatures. The CA and SC affirmed; Justice Leonen lamented the 'apathetic prosecution.' CJ agrees: the duo should simply have taken depositions of the Swiss officials they regularly visited, since 'one thing is knowing a fact, quite another to prove it in court using the stringent rules of evidence.'
